section_1.title: From ODEs to PDEs: The Concept of Multivariable Change
section_1.content: Briefly recap Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) where the function depends on one variable (like time). Introduce PDEs as equations involving functions of several variables (e.g., position x and time t) and their partial derivatives. Explain the transition from 'tracking a single point' to 'mapping a field'.
section_1.example: Visual comparison: An ODE tracks a single bead sliding on a wire; a PDE tracks the vibration of an entire guitar string.

section_2.title: The Heat Equation: Visualizing Diffusion
section_2.content: Introduce the Heat Equation: u_t = αu_xx. Explain that it describes how a quantity (like heat) spreads over space over time. Use an animation showing a hot spot on a metal rod flattening out into a smooth curve due to diffusion.
section_2.example: A cat sitting on a cold metal plate; the heat from the cat's paw slowly diffuses through the plate, modeled by the temperature gradient changing over time.

section_3.title: Boundary and Initial Conditions: Setting the Scene
section_3.content: Explain that a PDE alone has infinite solutions. To find a unique solution, we need: 1. Initial Conditions (what happens at t=0) and 2. Boundary Conditions (what happens at the edges of the domain).
section_3.example: Visualizing a swimming pool: The initial condition is the shape of the water ripple when a pebble drops, and the boundary condition is the pool wall where the wave reflects back.

section_4.title: The Wave Equation: Oscillations in Space-Time
section_4.content: Introduce the Wave Equation: u_tt = c²u_xx. Highlight the difference from the Heat Equation (second-order time derivative). Show how this produces periodic back-and-forth movement rather than smoothing out.
section_4.example: A plucked guitar string: The animation shows the displacement 'u' propagating as a wave front, illustrating how disturbances travel through a medium.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Real-World Impact
section_5.content: Summarize that PDEs are the 'language of nature', governing fluid dynamics, electromagnetism, and quantum mechanics. Encourage students to see the connection between spatial geometry and temporal change.
section_5.example: Summary visual: A montage of a satellite dish (waves), a weather map (fluid flow), and a bridge structure (stress distribution) to show the ubiquity of PDEs.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=20, color=WHITE, t2c={line: WHITE}) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)
